attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his signed post. The Hinton reference is a contrast, not a quotation of the claim.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will' prediction in the high-confidence list. The post's intro sets the horizon at end of 2025. The proposition matches the source.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: replacement means jobs actually lost to AI, 'few' means isolated cases, and no country restriction is added. It is not stretched for or against the speaker.

evidence.note: The RCR 2025 census covers UK hiring freezes amid shortages. It does not count AI-caused replacement and is UK only.
A 2025 preprint on whether AI could report normal chest X-rays on its own. It is about feasibility and does not measure displacement.

reviews.rationale: The 2025 horizon has passed. Neither item measures AI-caused radiologist replacement: e1 covers UK hiring freezes and shortages, and e2 is a feasibility discussion. Nothing shows substantial replacement, but the contract requires direct evidence that replacement was absent or isolated across the year, and the packet has none. The evidence does not settle the outcome.

attribution.note: Marcus's own retrospective statement in his signed post.

semantics.note: He reports on the status of an earlier hedged analogy ('might someday') and gives a vague view of risk. No new forecast is made, so the observation label is acceptable.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to turn the WeWork analogy into a definite event. 'Far from out of the woods' sets no risk threshold, so no scoring condition is available.

reviews.rationale: The statement combines a hedged analogy whose features are never specified with a vague description of continuing business risk. It gives no observable event or threshold to test, and the packet rightly contains no outcome evidence. This makes it untestable, so not_adjudicable.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assessment of his prediction about 2024.

semantics.note: A retrospective claim with the 'some folks but not all' qualifier kept. The self-graded 'partial credit' is evaluative and is rightly not scored.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: disappointment among some alongside continued enthusiasm among others in 2024. It adds no majority threshold, consistent with the qualifier.

evidence.note: The Deloitte mid-2024 survey reports challenges tempering leadership enthusiasm while investment kept rising. This shows disappointment coexisting with continued interest.
The BCG 2024 survey reports confidence and bullish views among many respondents. This supports the 'not all' part.

reviews.rationale: The claim is qualified: some people were disillusioned with AI in 2024 and others were not. Deloitte's 2024 survey documents tempered leadership enthusiasm (e9), and BCG's 2024 survey shows continued confidence among many respondents (e10). Together they meet the contract's support condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own prediction in his signed post.

semantics.note: 'Less than 10%' is a firm forecast for 2025. 'Probably less than 5%' is hedged and should not be scored; the proposition keeps that hedge.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair: actual replacement during 2025 against a global workforce, with only the 10% threshold firm.

evidence.note: The ILO study measures exposure to AI, not actual job losses, and says so explicitly.
Challenger counts about 55k announced AI-cited US layoffs in 2025. These are announcements by US employers only, not completed global replacements.
The NBER digest (May 2026) reports small employment effects in a four-country firm survey. That is firm-reported and net, not global gross replacement.

reviews.rationale: The 2025 horizon has passed. All three items are context: exposure indexes, announced US layoffs, and firm-reported net effects in four countries. They point to small effects, but none gives a representative estimate or credible upper bound for actual global AI replacement in 2025, which the contract requires. The packet does not settle the outcome.
